niche: Mind Hacks, AI Secrets, Bizarre Body Science & Hidden Power Dynamics

ideas.title: The 5000 Brain Glitch
ideas.angle: An interactive mental math challenge where the viewer adds numbers quickly in their head, only to be tricked by their brain's pattern-recognition into saying 5,000 when the answer is actually 4,100. This triggers a flood of 'I failed' or 'Wait, how?' comments.

hook.en: Calculate these numbers in your head now.

ideas.reason: Interactive math traps consistently achieve >100% APV because viewers re-watch to find where they made the mistake. The '5000 glitch' is a classic cognitive shortcut error that is virtually impossible to avoid on the first try.
sources: Cognitive Psychology: Shortcut processing in arithmetic (Heuristics and Biases)
The Stroop Effect & Numerical Cognition studies

ideas.title: The Forehead Dominance Hack
ideas.angle: A social power play showing the 'Social Power Gaze'—staring at the point between someone’s eyebrows during a conversation. It explains how this triggers a submissive biological response in the other person, making them lose their train of thought.

hook.en: Look here to win any argument.

ideas.reason: High-status social survival rules are currently trending in the 'sigma' and 'dark psychology' niches. It promises an immediate, 'unfair' advantage in social interactions, which drives high VVSA.
sources: The Definitive Book of Body Language (Allan & Barbara Pease)
Non-verbal communication research on eye-gaze and dominance

ideas.title: The 4-Swallow Challenge
ideas.angle: A physical impossibility test where the viewer is challenged to swallow four times in rapid succession. The video explains the biological 'refractory period' of the swallowing reflex that makes it feel like your throat is paralyzed.

hook.en: You cannot swallow four times fast.

ideas.reason: Physical 'body hacks' or 'impossible tests' have the highest VVSA because the viewer performs the action while the video is playing. This creates a high retention loop as they try to beat the biological limitation.
sources: Neurological refractory periods in involuntary muscle movements
